title: Remembering the Xenia Tornado
description: In a matter of minutes on the afternoon of April 3, 1974, the relative quiet on a spring day in the small southwestern Ohio town of Xenia was shattered. A powerful F-5 tornado tore a path of destruction. It killed 33 people and injured hundreds more. Survivors and National Guard members talk about their experiences on the 45th anniversary of the deadly tornado.
keywords: disaster response, tornado, Xenia, natural disaster, Ohio, Ohio National Guard

transcript.text: - And we could see things flipping around in it.
We thought it was newspapers, it was walls.
- The operator said, can't put any calls through
because that whole town's been destroyed.
- I had never seen anything like this in my life.
- [Narrator] In a matter of minutes
on the afternoon of April third 1974,
the relative quiet of a spring day
in the small Southwestern Ohio town of Xenia was shattered.
A powerful F5 tornado tore a path of destruction.
Homes and schools were leveled, businesses destroyed.
The nearby Ohio Army National Guard Armory was damaged.
Kathy Wilson was nine when the tornado touched down
near her family's home.
- Two blocks down from us was pretty well flattened.
So, that's how close it was.
- [Narrator] Her father Ray Kidd was working
as an aircraft mechanic at the Ohio Air National Guard's
178th Wing in Springfield.
He remembers jumping in his car to get home
to check on his family and the roadblocks he faced
like the derailed train that was spread across Main Street.
- I crawled under the train and I walked back up
and I could see the path of the tornado.
I knew that it couldn't'a missed our house.
- [Narrator] While his wife and two daughters
made it out safely, 33 people were killed that day.
Kidd and others from the 178th
were put on state active duty to help guard against looting
and assist in the recovery effort.
They were followed closely behind
by Ohio Army National Guard soldiers
on the ground and in the air.
- They had us go in,
out in sort of the rural areas
and go into farmhouses and things,
and we'd land and check for survivors
and see if people were injured and things like that.
- Guarding everything from pilferage.
Helping wherever we could.
Trying to get peoples' stuff out of the way.
We're moving bricks or boards or
furniture or whatever to try to get a hole through
so they can get in.
We transported people.
- [Narrator] Tragically a few days after the tornado,
two airmen from the 178th were killed
when fire raced through a downtown furniture store
they were guarding.
Ohio National Guard Troops continued to help
the residents of Xenia for several weeks.
- You felt like you were doing something worthwhile.
The people all were so appreciative of your part in it.
- [Narrator] There are still reminders of that day.
Parking lots where buildings once stood,
a memorial to those who lost their lives.
At the Greene County Historical Society
where Wilson is the Executive Director,
visitors can see some of the destruction
of the deadly twister and the resiliency
of the people who experienced it.
- Xenia itself was a different place.
It changed us
but it also brought the neighborhood closer together.
- It made me be very proud to be in the Guard.
And to be a part of
a big force that can do so much good.
